extracted.intended_audience: writers, critics, students, and general readers interested in narrative theory, storytelling, film and theatre
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for creating or assessing works that ask audiences to accept implausible or unreal premises (across literature, film, and theatre). Covers authorial techniques, psychological mechanisms, and debates about responsibility for plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infuse human interest and a semblance of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: If an author could infuse a 'human interest and a semblance of truth' into a story with implausible elements, the reader would willingly suspend judgement concerning the implausibility of the narrative. (Quoted from Coleridge's Biographia Literaria.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge's formulation stresses transferring 'human interest' from 'our inward nature' to the fantastic so that 'shadows of imagination' procure a 'willing suspension of disbelief for the moment, which constitutes poetic faith.' Examples: Coleridge's work in Lyrical Ballads and efforts to make fantastic elements feel truthful. Implication for writers: ground fantastical elements in recognizably human emotions, motives, or concerns so readers accept implausible events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain supernatural or implausible elements in plausible terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should attempt to explain supernatural characters and events in plausible terms so that implausible characters and events of the imagination can seem to be truthful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge advocated explaining supernatural elements to make them credible within the story. Practical guidance: provide plausible in-world rationale or contextualization for extraordinary events rather than presenting them as arbitrary. Anti-pattern: unexplained, arbitrary supernatural occurrences that break reader trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create internal consistency (secondary belief)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader must believe that what they read is true within the secondary reality of the fictional world; inner consistency of reality enables 'secondary belief' (Tolkien's paradigm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolkien argued that focusing on creating an internally consistent fictional world makes secondary belief possible and reduces the need for 'suspension of disbelief.' If internal consistency fails, readers must consciously suspend disbelief or disengage. Practical implication: rules, causal logic, and coherent worldbuilding that do not contradict themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the audience in a perceiving/engaged mode ('poetic faith')
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative value and engagement support a willing 'poetic faith'—when a person engages with a narrative the brain goes into a perceiving mode and assesses less critically; when engagement lapses the work's 'truth-value' is reevaluated (Norman N. Holland's neuroscientific theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain narrative hooks, emotional investment, sensory detail, and pacing to prevent the audience from switching to critical evaluation. Examples: continuous immersion in a scene keeps viewers/readers from interrupting their engagement to assess plausibility. Anti-pattern: breaks in engagement (poor pacing, intrusive errors) that trigger critical judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize medium limitations interfering with premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences often must overlook limitations of a medium (e.g., staged performance, early black-and-white film technical constraints) so these do not interfere with acceptance of the story's premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The burden falls on creators to present premises and technical choices that the audience can accept. In film, this means cinematography, acting, effects and staging should support the illusion rather than call attention to artifice. Anti-pattern: visible technical or presentational limitations that distract and break the fictional illusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cognitive estrangement strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Cognitive estrangement in fiction involves using a person's ignorance to promote suspension of disbelief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques that withhold or reshape familiar information (defamiliarization) can help audiences accept novel premises by preventing immediate real-world comparisons. Practical uses include selective revelation, worldbuilding that foregrounds difference, and presenting unfamiliar contexts so the audience temporarily accepts altered norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors should bear responsibility rather than placing burden solely on readers
rubrics_metrics.description: The later loose usage of 'suspension of disbelief' sometimes implies the burden is on the reader to achieve it; critics argue this unfairly shifts responsibility away from the writer to construct acceptable premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice: writers should craft believable premises, consistent internal rules, and credible character motivations instead of expecting readers to supply plausibility. Anti-pattern: leaning on a reader's willingness to 'just accept it' without sufficient in-text justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ dramatic and poetic conventions to facilitate suspension
rubrics_metrics.description: Live theatre and certain poetic forms rely on dramatic conventions whereby the audience ignores the unreality of fiction (Shakespearean prologues, theatrical conventions) to experience catharsis and accept narrative time/compression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit or implicit conventions (chorus, prologue, stylized staging) can signal to audiences how to interpret departures from realism. Use of conventional devices primes audiences to accept the premise and temporal or causal compressions. Anti-pattern: violating established conventions without providing alternative framing, which can confuse or alienate the audience.
